claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection appears capable of impacting cognition in some patients with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC).
source: Infection with the etiological agent of COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, appears capable of impacting cognition in some patients with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC).
evidence: This is stated as a known observation in the abstract, supported by the broader context of the study investigating neuropathophysiological consequences.

claim: Similar alterations of neuroinflammation occur in SARS-CoV-2, AD, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD individuals compared to age- and gender-matched neurological cases.
source: Here, we show similar alterations of neuroinflammation and blood–brain barrier integrity in SARS-CoV-2, AD, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD individuals.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by transcriptional and cellular data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Similar alterations of blood-brain barrier integrity occur in SARS-CoV-2, AD, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD individuals compared to age- and gender-matched neurological cases.
source: Here, we show similar alterations of neuroinflammation and blood–brain barrier integrity in SARS-CoV-2, AD, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD individuals.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by HIF-1α data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Distribution of microglial changes reflected by the increase in Iba-1 reveals nodular morphological alterations in SARS-CoV-2-infected AD individuals.
source: Distribution of microglial changes reflected by the increase in Iba-1 reveals nodular morphological alterations in SARS-CoV-2-infected AD individuals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemical data showing nodular lesions in Figure 5.

claim: HIF-1α is significantly upregulated in the context of SARS-CoV-2 infection in the same brain regions regardless of AD status.
source: Similarly, HIF-1α is significantly upregulated in the context of SARS-CoV-2 infection in the same brain regions regardless of AD status.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemical quantitation in Figure 6.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may be neuroinvasive, leading to neurological symptoms including anosmia, ageusia, cognitive functions, and cerebrovascular disorders.
source: Previous evidence tentatively suggests that SARS-CoV-2 may be neuroinvasive, leading to a vast array of neurological symptoms, including anosmia, ageusia, cognitive functions, and cerebrovascular disorders (Desforges et al., 2014; Hingorani et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Desforges et al., 2014; Hingorani et al., 2022).

claim: Neurological complications of SARS-CoV-2 infection manifest with increased severity related to age and shared medical history of metabolic disorders and other vascular risk factors.
source: Neurological complications of SARS-CoV-2 infection manifest with increased severity related to age and shared medical history of metabolic disorders and other vascular risk factors (Divani et al., 2020; Chou et al., 2021; Sullivan and Fischer, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Divani et al., 2020; Chou et al., 2021; Sullivan and Fischer, 2021).

claim: HCoV-OC43 can lead to glutamate excitotoxicity and neuronal degradation in mice through cytokine production.
source: Some strains within the coronavirus family are implicated in neuronal degeneration, such as HCoV-OC43, which can lead to glutamate excitotoxicity and neuronal degradation in mice through cytokine production (Jacomy et al., 2010; Brison et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Jacomy et al., 2010; Brison et al., 2011).

claim: Secretion of cytokines and chemokines from the periphery allows the recruitment of leukocytes and other cells to specific tissues.
source: While it is currently unknown whether neurological manifestations of SARS-CoV-2 infection arise solely from systemic inflammation in the periphery or brain infiltration, it is well established that secretion of cytokines and chemokines from the periphery allows the recruitment of leukocytes and other cells to specific tissues (Bauer et al., 2022; Prinz and Priller, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bauer et al., 2022; Prinz and Priller, 2017).

claim: Peripheral immune response is speculated to accelerate blood-brain barrier disruption and may potentially damage cells within the central nervous system.
source: This type of immune response is speculated to accelerate blood–brain barrier (BBB) disruption and may potentially damage cells within the central nervous system (CNS) (de Erausquin et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature (de Erausquin et al., 2021) and is presented as speculation.

claim: Leukocyte infiltration, BBB dysregulation, and microglial activation are observed in Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Such effects are similar to neuropathology seen in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative disorders, where leukocyte infiltration, BBB dysregulation, and microglial activation are observed.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about AD and neurodegenerative disorders.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may accelerate the onset and severity of cognitive decline or AD in susceptible individuals.
source: Thus, it is possible that SARS-CoV-2 may accelerate the onset and severity of cognitive decline or AD in susceptible individuals (Meinhardt et al., 2021; Mhatre et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is presented as a possibility supported by citations to previous literature (Meinhardt et al., 2021; Mhatre et al., 2015).

claim: Each study group comprises an equal number of age-matched male and female patients with an average age of 79.6 among groups.
source: Each group comprises an equal number of age-matched male and female patients, ensuring equal distribution with an average age of 79.6 among groups.
evidence: This is a description of the study design and demographics.

claim: All AD individuals have postmortem ABC scores indicative of AD.
source: Medical records indicate that all AD individuals have postmortem ABC scores indicative of AD (Supplementary file 2), where A is a measure of amyloid β deposition, B is a measure of neurofibrillary degeneration based on the Braak and Brook score, and C is scored based on neuritic plaques outlined by the Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease diagnosis (CERAD) (Kovacs and Gelpi, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by medical records data and a citation explaining the ABC scoring system (Kovacs and Gelpi, 2012).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by diagnostic polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
source: SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by diagnostic polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
evidence: This describes the method used to confirm SARS-CoV-2 infection in the study subjects.

claim: All patients in the SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD groups were symptomatic, admitted to the hospital, and received oxygen supplementation.
source: Within the SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD groups, all patients were symptomatic, admitted to the hospital, and received oxygen supplementation by ventilator or cannula with disease onset to death occurring on average 27 d after diagnosis for patients with SARS-CoV-2 only and 32 d after diagnosis in infected AD patients (Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by patient medical records data.

claim: Disease onset to death occurred on average 27 days after diagnosis for patients with SARS-CoV-2 only.
source: Within the SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD groups, all patients were symptomatic, admitted to the hospital, and received oxygen supplementation by ventilator or cannula with disease onset to death occurring on average 27 d after diagnosis for patients with SARS-CoV-2 only and 32 d after diagnosis in infected AD patients (Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by patient medical records data.

claim: Disease onset to death occurred on average 32 days after diagnosis in SARS-CoV-2-infected AD patients.
source: Within the SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD groups, all patients were symptomatic, admitted to the hospital, and received oxygen supplementation by ventilator or cannula with disease onset to death occurring on average 27 d after diagnosis for patients with SARS-CoV-2 only and 32 d after diagnosis in infected AD patients (Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by patient medical records data.

claim: Blood specimens indicate several laboratory features of severe COVID-19, such as increased C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6).
source: Blood specimens were collected and indicate several laboratory features of severe COVID-19 (Supplementary file 2), such as increased C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) (Lampart et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by blood specimen data and a citation to previous literature (Lampart et al., 2022).

claim: In the AD group in cortical BA9, 287 genes were upregulated and 131 genes were downregulated.
source: In the AD group, 287 genes were upregulated and 131 genes were downregulated (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the SARS-CoV-2 group in cortical BA9, 179 genes were upregulated and 426 genes were downregulated.
source: In the SARS-CoV-2 group, 179 genes were upregulated and 426 genes were downregulated (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the SARS-CoV-2-infected AD group in cortical BA9, 813 genes were upregulated and 611 genes were downregulated.
source: The volcano plot distribution of gene transcripts of SARS-CoV-2-infected AD cases compared to neurological controls (Figure 1C) revealed 38,021 genes and showed 813 genes were upregulated and 611 genes were downregulated using the same cutoff for significance (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: In the AD group in HF, 304 genes were upregulated and 214 genes were downregulated.
source: In the AD group, 304 genes were upregulated and 214 genes were downregulated (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In the SARS-CoV-2 group in HF, 230 genes were upregulated and 464 genes were downregulated.
source: In the SARS-CoV-2 group, 230 genes were upregulated and 464 genes were downregulated (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In the SARS-CoV-2-infected AD group in HF, 466 genes were upregulated and 582 genes were downregulated.
source: Additionally, in the SARS-CoV-2-infected AD group, 466 genes were upregulated and 582 genes were downregulated (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The AD and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD comparisons were strikingly similar in both BA9 and HF.
source: While all three comparisons (AD versus control, SARS-CoV-2 versus control, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD versus control) showed generally the same trends, the AD and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD comparisons were strikingly similar in both BA9 (Figure 2A) and HF (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: RRHO analysis comparing SARS-CoV-2 and AD cases reveals a positive correlation between the AD and SARS-CoV-2 groups in the cortical BA9.
source: Rank-rank hypergeometric overlap (RRHO) analysis comparing SARS-CoV-2 and AD cases also reveals a positive correlation between the AD and SARS-CoV-2 groups in the cortical BA9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) as well as in the HF (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), although to a lesser extent than in the cortical BA9.
evidence: This is supported by RRHO analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: RRHO analysis comparing SARS-CoV-2 and AD cases reveals a positive correlation between the AD and SARS-CoV-2 groups in the HF, although to a lesser extent than in the cortical BA9.
source: Rank-rank hypergeometric overlap (RRHO) analysis comparing SARS-CoV-2 and AD cases also reveals a positive correlation between the AD and SARS-CoV-2 groups in the cortical BA9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) as well as in the HF (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), although to a lesser extent than in the cortical BA9.
evidence: This is supported by RRHO analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In cortical BA9, AD, SARS-CoV-2, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD individuals shared 410 upregulated genes and 269 downregulated genes from 679 expressed genes.
source: Comparing these shared genes within the cortical BA9, we find that AD, SARS-CoV-2, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD individuals shared 410 upregulated genes and 269 downregulated genes from 679 expressed genes (Figure 2C and Source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by IPA filtering analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the HF, AD, SARS-CoV-2, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD individuals share 211 upregulated genes and 148 downregulated genes from 359 differentially expressed genes.
source: In the HF, we found that the three groups share 211 upregulated genes and 148 downregulated genes from 359 differentially expressed genes (Figure 2D and Source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by IPA filtering analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Several pathways, including neuroinflammation, TREM1, and cell senescence, show increased activation in the AD, SARS-CoV-2, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD groups in cortical BA9.
source: Within the cortical BA9 region (Figure 3A), for example, several pathways, including neuroinflammation, TREM1, and cell senescence, show increased activation in the AD, SARS-CoV-2, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD groups.
evidence: This is supported by IPA pathway analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TREM1 signaling is the most highly activated pathway in the cortical BA9 dataset.
source: TREM1 signaling, the most highly activated pathway in this dataset (Figure 3A and B), is expressed primarily on myeloid cells, such as macrophages and microglia, and is involved in pro-inflammatory immune responses (de Oliveira Matos et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by IPA pathway analysis shown in Figure 3A and 3B, and a citation to previous literature (de Oliveira Matos et al., 2020).

claim: TREM1 is expressed primarily on myeloid cells, such as macrophages and microglia, and is involved in pro-inflammatory immune responses.
source: TREM1 signaling, the most highly activated pathway in this dataset (Figure 3A and B), is expressed primarily on myeloid cells, such as macrophages and microglia, and is involved in pro-inflammatory immune responses (de Oliveira Matos et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature (de Oliveira Matos et al., 2020).

claim: Age-associated cellular senescence occurs during cellular stress due to inflammation, including that caused by viral infections, leading to a senescence-associated secretory phenotype such as metalloproteinases (MMPs) and inflammatory cytokines.
source: Although age-associated cellular senescence (Figure 3A) is a natural process where telomeres shorten over time, this process also occurs during cellular stress due to inflammation, including that caused by viral infections, leading to a senescence-associated secretory phenotype such as metalloproteinases (MMPs), and inflammatory cytokines (Lee et al., 2021; Coppé et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature (Lee et al., 2021; Coppé et al., 2010).

claim: SNARE pathway shows decreased activation in the AD and SARS-CoV-2 groups in cortical BA9, with the most significant reduction seen in the SARS-CoV-2-infected AD cases group.
source: Another pathway of interest, SNARE, shows decreased activation in the AD and SARS-CoV-2 groups (Figure 3A), with the most significant reduction seen in the SARS-CoV-2-infected AD cases group.
evidence: This is supported by IPA pathway analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SNARE proteins play an essential role in neurotransmitter release, and altered function is implicated in the pathophysiology of neurodegenerative diseases such as AD.
source: SNARE proteins play an essential role in neurotransmitter release, and altered function is implicated in the pathophysiology of neurodegenerative diseases such as AD, where SNARE proteins affect β-amyloid (Aβ) accumulation and cytoplasmic transport of neurofibrillary tangles (Margiotta, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature (Margiotta, 2021).

claim: In the HF, interleukin-8 (IL-8) and ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) signaling is upregulated in AD, SARS-CoV-2, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD groups.
source: Within the HF (Figure 4A), for example, interleukin-8 (IL-8) another neuroinflammatory pathway, and ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) signaling is upregulated in AD, SARS-CoV-2, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD groups, while cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) is also upregulated in the SARS-CoV-2 groups but downregulated in AD-only (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by IPA pathway analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CREB is upregulated in the SARS-CoV-2 groups but downregulated in AD-only in the HF.
source: Within the HF (Figure 4A), for example, interleukin-8 (IL-8) another neuroinflammatory pathway, and ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) signaling is upregulated in AD, SARS-CoV-2, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD groups, while cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) is also upregulated in the SARS-CoV-2 groups but downregulated in AD-only (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by IPA pathway analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: IL-8 has several important roles, including endothelial cell migration and chemoattraction of neutrophils.
source: IL-8 has several important roles, including endothelial cell migration and chemoattraction of neutrophils (Manda-Handzlik and Demkow, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature (Manda-Handzlik and Demkow, 2019).

claim: IL-8 aids cell migration by enhancing the expression of molecules such as MMP-2, MMP-9, involved in BBB integrity and induction of neuronal apoptosis, and VEGF-A, involved in vascular permeability and angiogenesis.
source: One way IL-8 aids cell migration is by enhancing the expression of molecules such as MMP-2, MMP-9, involved in BBB integrity and induction of neuronal apoptosis, and VEGF-A, involved in vascular permeability and angiogenesis, thus having a potential effect on vascular damage (Lugano et al., 2020; Jian et al., 2018; Licht and Keshet, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature (Lugano et al., 2020; Jian et al., 2018; Licht and Keshet, 2013).

claim: CNTF signaling aids in the prevention of neuronal degeneration after injury and is neuroprotective in diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: CNTF signaling aids in the prevention of neuronal degeneration after injury and is neuroprotective in diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Pasquin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature (Pasquin et al., 2015).

claim: CREB signaling modulates processes in consolidating memory and information processing and is inhibited in AD.
source: Interestingly, CREB signaling modulates processes in consolidating memory and information processing and is inhibited in AD (Amidfar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature (Amidfar et al., 2020).

claim: A reduction in CREB signaling is seen in AD individuals in the HF, but this effect is reversed in SARS-CoV-2-infected AD individuals.
source: Consistent with these findings, we also see a reduction in CREB signaling in the AD individuals; however, this effect is reversed in SARS-CoV-2-infected AD individuals in the HF.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upregulation of integrin signaling and nerve growth factor (NGF) signaling occur in both cortical BA9 and HF tissue in all SARS-CoV-2, AD and SARS-CoV-2 infected AD groups.
source: Additionally, upregulation of integrin signaling and nerve growth factor (NGF) signaling occur in both cortical BA9 and HF tissue (Figures 3B and 4B) in all SARS-CoV-2, AD and SARS-CoV-2 infected AD groups.
evidence: This is supported by IPA pathway analysis shown in Figures 3B and 4B.

claim: NGF signaling is critical for the survival of neurons, and alterations of NGF signaling has been implicated in neurodegenerative disorders such as AD.
source: Neuronal function shown by the upregulation of NGF signaling is critical for the survival of neurons, and alterations of NGF signaling has been implicated in neurodegenerative disorders such as AD (Eu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature (Eu et al., 2021).

claim: Integrin signaling is used for a diverse array of functions within the CNS via cell-to-cell and cell-to-extracellular matrix interactions.
source: Integrin signaling is used for a diverse array of functions within the CNS via cell-to-cell and cell-to-extracellular matrix interactions (Ikeshima-Kataoka et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature (Ikeshima-Kataoka et al., 2022).

claim: Microglia in AD, SARS-CoV-2, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD cases are more numerous and display an activated phenotype, with retracted, thickened processes and enlarged somas, compared to neurological controls.
source: Compared to neurological controls, microglia in AD, SARS-CoV-2, and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD cases are more numerous and display an activated phenotype, with retracted, thickened processes and enlarged somas (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Microglia appear to accumulate around blood vessels in the context of AD and SARS-CoV-2 groups but not in unaffected neurological controls brain.
source: Microglia also appear to accumulate around blood vessels in the context of AD and SARS-CoV-2 groups but not in unaffected neurological controls brain (Figure 5E–H), suggesting that factors at the level of the BBB may participate in microglial activation.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: Factors at the level of the BBB may participate in microglial activation.
source: Microglia also appear to accumulate around blood vessels in the context of AD and SARS-CoV-2 groups but not in unaffected neurological controls brain (Figure 5E–H), suggesting that factors at the level of the BBB may participate in microglial activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of microglial accumulation around blood vessels.

claim: Microglial nodules were seen in all conditions but appeared larger and more frequently in infection compared to AD-only and controls.
source: Microglial nodules, which are commonly observed in neuroinflammatory disease, were seen in all conditions but appeared larger and more frequently in infection compared to AD-only and controls (Figure 5I–L).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 5I-L.

claim: When detectable, SARS-CoV-2 appears to be restricted to the endothelium.
source: When detectable, SARS-CoV-2 appears to be restricted to the endothelium (Figure 5G, H, K and L) and did not colocalize with Iba-1 or glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP; data not shown), suggesting that neither microglia nor astrocytes harbor productive virus.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 5G, H, K and L.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 did not colocalize with Iba-1 or glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), suggesting that neither microglia nor astrocytes harbor productive virus.
source: When detectable, SARS-CoV-2 appears to be restricted to the endothelium (Figure 5G, H, K and L) and did not colocalize with Iba-1 or glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP; data not shown), suggesting that neither microglia nor astrocytes harbor productive virus.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of colocalization observed in immunohistochemical analysis.

claim: There is a statistically significant increase in the number of microglia in AD alone in the HF.
source: A statistically significant increase in the number of microglia occurs in AD alone in the HF and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD cases in both the HF and cortical BA9 (Figure 5M and O).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5M and O.

claim: There is a statistically significant increase in the number of microglia in SARS-CoV-2-infected AD cases in both the HF and cortical BA9.
source: A statistically significant increase in the number of microglia occurs in AD alone in the HF and SARS-CoV-2-infected AD cases in both the HF and cortical BA9 (Figure 5M and O).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5M and O.

claim: An increase in the frequency of nodular lesions was seen with SARS-CoV-2 infection, with and without AD, in both brain regions assessed.
source: An increase in the frequency of nodular lesions was seen with SARS-CoV-2 infection, with and without AD, in both brain regions assessed. However, a statistically significant increase in nodular lesions is present in SARS-CoV-2-infected AD cases (Figure 5P–R).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5P-R.

claim: A statistically significant increase in nodular lesions is present in SARS-CoV-2-infected AD cases.
source: An increase in the frequency of nodular lesions was seen with SARS-CoV-2 infection, with and without AD, in both brain regions assessed. However, a statistically significant increase in nodular lesions is present in SARS-CoV-2-infected AD cases (Figure 5P–R).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5P-R.

claim: Upregulation and stabilization of HIF-1α are most pronounced in the context of SARS-CoV-2 infection, regardless of AD status in cortical BA9 and HF.
source: Upregulation and stabilization of HIF-1α are most pronounced in the context of SARS-CoV-2 infection, regardless of AD status in cortical BA9 (Figure 6A–D) and HF (Figure 6E–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 6A-H.

claim: HIF-1α is only slightly elevated in cortical BA9 of AD patients compared to age-matched neurological controls.
source: Nonbiased area positivity quantitation revealed that HIF-1α is only slightly elevated in cortical BA9 of AD patients compared to age-matched neurological controls (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claim: A greater increase in HIF-1α occurs in the HF from SARS-CoV-2 individuals, with and without AD.
source: In contrast, a greater increase occurs in the HF from SARS-CoV-2 individuals, with and without AD.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of HIF-1α in the manuscript.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 only samples showed a significant increase in HIF-1α of cortical BA9 compared to controls.
source: SARS-CoV-2 only samples showed a significant increase in HIF-1α of cortical BA9 compared to controls (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6I-K.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 and AD-infected individuals share similar alterations of regulatory patterns of immune-inflammatory pathways and pathways involved with cognition.
source: The finding from our study suggests that SARS-CoV-2 and AD-infected individuals share similar alterations of regulatory patterns of immune-inflammatory pathways and pathways involved with cognition as suggested by recent meta-analyses showing shared neuroinflammation and microvascular injury, in particular AD and SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals (Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the study's findings and a citation to previous literature (Zhou et al., 2021).

claim: Zhou and colleagues found a significant overlap in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) monocytes and markers in AD and COVID-19.
source: Additionally, Zhou and colleagues found a significant overlap in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) monocytes and markers in AD and COVID-19, which also occurs in our dataset (Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature (Zhou et al., 2021) and comparison to the current dataset.

claim: The similarities of transcriptional profiles and cellular pathophysiology in SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals support the potential role of SARS-CoV-2 infection on the CNS, leading to neuro-PASC symptoms such as brain fog and memory loss.
source: The similarities of transcriptional profiles and cellular pathophysiology in SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals support the potential role of SARS-CoV-2 infection on the CNS, leading to neuro-PASC symptoms such as brain fog and memory loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings on transcriptional and cellular similarities.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 generates a similar neuroinflammatory environment in neurodegenerative disorders like AD.
source: Notably, our study identifies similar neuroinflammatory profiles in SARS-CoV-2, AD, and AD SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals at the transcriptional and cellular levels in both the cortical BA9 and HF brain regions. This suggests that SARS-CoV-2 generates a similar neuroinflammatory environment in neurodegenerative disorders like AD.
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings on neuroinflammatory profiles.

claim: Microglia nodule formation is present in some neurodegenerative diseases, such as MS, and viral infections, such as herpes simplex virus (HSV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).
source: Microglia nodule formation is present in some neurodegenerative diseases, such as MS, and viral infections, such as herpes simplex virus (HSV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (Tröscher et al., 2019; Fischer-Smith, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature (Tröscher et al., 2019; Fischer-Smith, 2001).

claim: Nodular formation is initially characterized by abundant presence of activated microglia and innate immune factors leading to Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling and upregulations of inflammasome genes, leading to T cell stimulation and ultimately the destruction of neurons.
source: A potentially compounding finding is the nodular formation that is initially characterized by abundant presence of activated microglia and innate immune factors leading to Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling and upregulations of inflammasome genes, leading to T cell stimulation and ultimately the destruction of neurons (Tröscher et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature (Tröscher et al., 2019).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 further promotes neuroinflammation in AD, which likely advances the progression and severity of CNS disease in these individuals.
source: This suggests that SARS-CoV-2 further promotes neuroinflammation in AD, which likely advances the progression and severity of CNS disease in these individuals.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased nodular lesions in SARS-CoV-2-infected AD cases.

claim: Patients 65 years or older with SARS-CoV-2 were at an increased risk for a new AD diagnosis within a year of their SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis, with the most significant risk seen among those 85 years and older.
source: Interestingly, a large retrospective study of patients 65 years or older revealed that patients with SARS-CoV-2 were at an increased risk for a new AD diagnosis within a year of their SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis, with the most significant risk seen among those 85 years and older (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature (Wang et al., 2022).

claim: Preexisting inflammation in the brain, which is seen in the context of 'normal' aging, may play a critical role in promoting or advancing AD progression.
source: This may underscore the critical role of preexisting inflammation in the brain, which is seen in the context of 'normal' aging, in promoting or advancing AD progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased risk of AD diagnosis in older SARS-CoV-2 patients.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may cause cognitive deficits via regulation of pathways associated with cognition and neuroinflammation.
source: Our findings also support the notion that SARS-CoV-2 may cause cognitive deficits via regulation of pathways associated with cognition and neuroinflammation.
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings on pathway regulation.

claim: Changes in the transcriptional regulation of SNARE and NGF pathways suggest impaired neuronal health and function, presumably negatively impacting cognitive function.
source: Here, we show changes in the transcriptional regulation of SNARE and NGF pathways, suggesting impaired neuronal health and function, presumably negatively impacting cognitive function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed changes in SNARE and NGF pathway regulation.

claim: Potential damage to the vasculature occurs via increased regulation of HIF-1α, integrin signaling, and IL-8 signaling.
source: We also observed potential damage to the vasculature via increased regulation of HIF-1α, integrin signaling, and IL-8 signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed upregulation of these pathways.

claim: Vascular damage by SARS-CoV-2, as assessed by HIF-1α, is observed in non-human primates that were euthanized at designated end-of-life time points precluding breathing intervention.
source: It is important to note the possibility of vascular damage due to ventilation prior to death in SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals; however, vascular damage by SARS-CoV-2, as assessed by HIF-1α, is observed in non-human primates that were euthanized at designated end-of-life time points precluding breathing intervention (Rutkai et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature (Rutkai et al., 2022).

claim: Vascular damage findings may point to a possible route for lymphocyte transmigration following chemoattractant gradients such as IL-8 and enhancement of MMPs and VEGF, which are aided by integrins such as cellular adhesion molecules such as ICAM-1.
source: These findings may point to a possible route for lymphocyte transmigration following chemoattractant gradients such as IL-8 and enhancement of MMPs and VEGF, which are aided by integrins such as cellular adhesion molecules such as ICAM-1 and are implicated with inflammatory signal transduction (Patarroyo et al., 1990; Bui et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed pathway changes and supported by citations to previous literature (Patarroyo et al., 1990; Bui et al., 2020).

claim: Lymphocyte transmigration leads to T cell activation, which may be responsible for the observed inflammatory environment.
source: This process leads to T cell activation, which may be responsible for the observed inflammatory environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed pathway changes.

claim: Transcriptional data showed an abundant upregulation of TLRs (TLRs 1, 5, 7, and 8) related to the inflammasome.
source: Our transcriptional data showed an abundant upregulation of TLRs (TLRs 1, 5, 7, and 8) related to the inflammasome.
evidence: This is supported by the transcriptional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Further analysis of this dataset indicated the potential role for T cells through IL-7 pathway activation and CD86 upregulation.
